ready_drafts.title: Warm words on the road
ready_drafts.literal_meaning: Sweet-speaking Radha: when one goes to the house, she does not speak; on the road, such affection.
ready_drafts.explanation: The praise in “sweet-speaking” is undercut by the change of setting. On the road there is a warm reception; at the house there is not even conversation. The linked dictionary definition includes flattering words that conceal a different intention, so the contrast is sharper than a simple difference between a busy and a free moment. The line can tease or reproach warmth that seems to depend on where it is displayed. It does not tell us who visits the house or what relationship the visitor has to Radha. Our present-day application concerns inconsistent welcome, not a rule about women or a story about a deity.
ready_drafts.meaning_odia: ବାଟରେ ଦେଖାହେଲେ ଏତେ ଶରଧା, ଘରକୁ ଗଲେ ପଦେ କଥା ନାହିଁ—ସ୍ଥାନ ବଦଳିବା ସାଙ୍ଗରେ ଆଚରଣ ବଦଳିଯାଉଛି। ଏହି ଓଲଟା ଦେଖାଇ “କଅଁଳକହୀ” ପ୍ରଶଂସାଟି କଟାକ୍ଷ ହୋଇଯାଏ। ସଂଯୁକ୍ତ ଅଭିଧାନ ଶବ୍ଦରେ ମନରେ କପଟ ରଖି ମିଠା କଥା କହିବାର ଅର୍ଥ ମଧ୍ୟ ଅଛି। ଦେଖାସାକ୍ଷାତରେ ଆଦର ଦେଖାଇ ପାଖକୁ ଆସିଲେ ମୁହଁ ଫେରାଇବାକୁ ଏହି କଥାରେ ଧରିହୁଏ। କିଏ ଘରକୁ ଗଲେ ବା ରାଧାଙ୍କ ସହ ତାଙ୍କର କି ସମ୍ପର୍କ, ପଦଟି ସେ କଥା କହେନାହିଁ।
ready_drafts.english_summary: A warm greeting in one setting rings hollow when it turns into silence in another.
ready_drafts.odia_summary: ବାଟର ଆଦର ଘରେ ନିରବତା ହେଲେ ମିଠା କଥାର ଅସଙ୍ଗତି ଧରାପଡ଼େ।
ready_drafts.usage_example: Original imagined example: A neighbour repeatedly welcomes someone warmly at the market and invites them to drop by. When the visitor arrives at the agreed time, the neighbour will not acknowledge them. Later, the visitor quotes the saying to a friend with a rueful laugh. This invented scene illustrates the contrast; it is not the source’s occasion.
ready_drafts.cultural_context: Radha is the name in the wording; no mythological identity, romance or biography is established.8859 is lexical context only, not another full-saying witness. The visitor and relationship remain unspecified. Teasing force follows the source contrast and linked flattering-speech definition; contemporary situation is editorial.

ready_drafts.title: A name for what?
ready_drafts.literal_meaning: Have a temple built and your name spreads; defecate on the road and your name spreads.
ready_drafts.explanation: The same phrase, “your name spreads”, carries two very different kinds of attention. Building a temple supplies the respectable image; fouling the road abruptly drags it down into coarse comedy. The dictionary places the saying under notoriety, after a separate sense for good reputation. Being talked about is therefore not enough to tell whether someone is admired or condemned. In an editorial everyday use, the line can puncture a boast about publicity by asking what earned it. Its shock is part of the contrast, not an instruction to humiliate a person or a claim about a particular temple builder.
ready_drafts.meaning_odia: ଦେଉଳ ତୋଳାଇଲେ ଲୋକେ ନାଁ କହନ୍ତି, ବାଟ ଅପରିଷ୍କାର କଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ନାଁ କହନ୍ତି—କିନ୍ତୁ ଦୁଇଥର କହିବାର ଅର୍ଥ ଏକ ନୁହେଁ। ସମ୍ମାନର ଚିତ୍ର ପଛକୁ ହଠାତ୍ ଏମିତି ଅଶୋଭନ କାମ ଆଣିବାରେ ଥଟ୍ଟାର ଝଟକା ଅଛି। ଅଭିଧାନ ମଧ୍ୟ ସୁଖ୍ୟାତି ଓ ଅପଯଶକୁ ଅଲଗା ଅର୍ଥରେ ରଖିଛି। ତେଣୁ କେତେ ଲୋକ ମୋ କଥା କହୁଛନ୍ତି ବୋଲି ଗର୍ବ କରିବା ପୂର୍ବରୁ କାହିଁକି କହୁଛନ୍ତି, ସେ ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ ଉଠେ। ନାଁ ହେବା ଓ ଭଲ ନାଁ ହେବାର ତଫାତକୁ ଏହି କଟାକ୍ଷ ମନେ ପକାଏ।
ready_drafts.english_summary: Attention alone cannot distinguish an admired reputation from notoriety.
ready_drafts.odia_summary: ନାଁ ହେବା ମାତ୍ରେ ସୁନାମ ହୁଏନାହିଁ; କେଉଁ କାମ ପାଇଁ ହେଲା, ସେଇଟି ଅସଲ କଥା।
ready_drafts.usage_example: Original imagined example: After a noisy argument at a neighbourhood meeting, a participant boasts that everyone is talking about him. A friend quotes the saying and asks whether he wanted to be remembered for the quarrel or for helping solve the problem. No actual meeting or person is being described.
ready_drafts.cultural_context: The coarse bodily verb is retained in the exact quotation and literal translation. The example uses a non-bodily modern situation. The Radhanath quotation in the preceding dictionary sense is a separate named literary example and is not presented as the author of this saying.

ready_drafts.title: Counting every piece, spending twice
ready_drafts.literal_meaning: The piece-counter uses up twice as much.
ready_drafts.explanation: The dictionary’s piece-counter is someone so miserly with food that each cut piece is counted before it is handed to the cook. The saying answers that anxious control with a reversal: the supposed saver ends up using twice as much. “Twice” gives the rebuke its bite; the source supplies no measured account or explanation of how the loss occurs. One editorial application is to a petty economy whose inconvenience creates more expense. The target is grasping control, not careful budgeting when resources are genuinely limited.
ready_drafts.meaning_odia: ରାନ୍ଧୁଣିଙ୍କୁ ଦେବା ଆଗରୁ ଖାଦ୍ୟର ପ୍ରତି ଖଣ୍ଡ ଗଣୁଥିବା କୃପଣଙ୍କୁ ଅଭିଧାନ “ଖଣ୍ଡ଼ିଗଣିଆଁ” କହିଛି। ଏତେ ହିସାବ ରଖି ମଧ୍ୟ ତାଙ୍କର ଦୁଇଗୁଣ ସରେ—ଏହି ଓଲଟା ଫଳରେ କଥାର ମଜା। କେମିତି ଦୁଇଗୁଣ ଖର୍ଚ୍ଚ ହେଲା, ଉତ୍ସ କୌଣସି ଘଟଣା ଦେଇନାହିଁ; ସଂଖ୍ୟାଟି କଟାକ୍ଷକୁ ଜୋର ଦିଏ। ଅଳ୍ପ ବଞ୍ଚାଇବାର ଜିଦ୍‌ରେ ଏମିତି ଅସୁବିଧା ତିଆରି ହୋଇପାରେ, ଯାହା ପାଇଁ ପରେ ଅଧିକ ଦେବାକୁ ପଡ଼େ। ଅଭାବରେ ସାବଧାନ ହୋଇ ଚଳିବାକୁ ନୁହେଁ, ଏଠାରେ ଅତି କୃପଣ ନିୟନ୍ତ୍ରଣକୁ ହସରେ ଧରାଯାଇଛି।
ready_drafts.english_summary: A miser’s minute control is mocked as an economy that can cost more.
ready_drafts.odia_summary: ପ୍ରତି ଖଣ୍ଡ ବଞ୍ଚାଇବାର କୃପଣତା ଶେଷରେ ଅଧିକ ଖର୍ଚ୍ଚର କାରଣ ହେବା ଉପରେ କଟାକ୍ଷ।
ready_drafts.usage_example: Original imagined example: For a shared event, an organiser insists on buying too few paper cups to save a little. When they run out, a volunteer makes a second trip and pays more for a small packet. Someone quotes the saying about the piece-counter. The cups and extra trip are an invented illustration, not the dictionary’s story.
ready_drafts.cultural_context: The source explicitly defines food-related miserliness. The broader petty-economy application is editorial. No quantitative spending law, nutritional instruction or judgement of people living in poverty is implied.

ready_drafts.title: Soft ground invites another pass
ready_drafts.literal_meaning: When they find it soft, they plough it a second time.
ready_drafts.explanation: The source places this line under “soft”, while the linked word dohada means a second tilling. That gives the saying a concrete repeated action: easy ground invites another pass of the plough. An editorial social reading hears a warning about someone taking further advantage when another person yields. It is a possible application of the image, not a separate traditional-use gloss supplied by this entry. The line need not make kindness a fault; the question is whether a concession is being treated as permission to keep pressing.
ready_drafts.meaning_odia: ନରମ ମିଳିଲେ ଆଉ ଥରେ ଚଷନ୍ତି—ଏଠାରେ ଏକ କାମ ସହଜ ହେବାରୁ ତାକୁ ପୁଣି କରିବାର ଚିତ୍ର ଅଛି। “ଦୋହଡ଼” ଅର୍ଥ ଦ୍ୱିତୀୟ ଥର ହଳ କରିବା ବୋଲି ସଂଯୁକ୍ତ ଅଭିଧାନ ଶବ୍ଦ ସ୍ପଷ୍ଟ କରେ। ଲୋକସମ୍ପର୍କରେ ଏହାକୁ ପଢ଼ିଲେ, ଜଣେ ଥରେ ଛାଡ଼ ଦେଲେ ଆଉ ଅଧିକ ଚାପ ଦେବାର କଥା ମନକୁ ଆସେ। ଏହା ଚିତ୍ରକୁ ଧରି ଆମର ପ୍ରୟୋଗମୂଳକ ପାଠ; ଉତ୍ସ ଅଲଗା ସାମାଜିକ ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଦେଇନାହିଁ। ସାହାଯ୍ୟ କରିବା ଭୁଲ ନୁହେଁ, କିନ୍ତୁ ଗୋଟିଏ ଛାଡ଼କୁ ସବୁବେଳର ଅଧିକାର କରିନେଲେ ସୀମା କେଉଁଠି ରହିବ?
ready_drafts.english_summary: In one social reading, an initial concession encourages someone to press for more.
ready_drafts.odia_summary: ଥରେ ଛାଡ଼ ପାଇ ଆଉ ଅଧିକ ଚାପ ଦେବାକୁ ଏହି ଚିତ୍ରରେ ପଢ଼ିହୁଏ।
ready_drafts.usage_example: Original imagined example: A colleague agrees to cover one shift. The same coworker then assumes they will cover the following weekend too, without asking. A friend quotes the saying, and the colleague clarifies that the first favour was for one day. This workplace use is editorial, not an attested origin.
ready_drafts.cultural_context: 199397 establishes second tilling only and is a context-only citation. The social application is explicitly editorial; no agricultural advice, rule about all generous people or documented origin is asserted.

ready_drafts.title: Can dew fill the pot?
ready_drafts.literal_meaning: Can a pot be filled by collecting dew?
ready_drafts.explanation: The question sets tiny drops against a vessel that needs filling. The dictionary describes collecting dew and compares a Hindi proverb about licking dew not satisfying thirst. The force is a challenge to adequacy: is what is being gathered enough for the need at hand? In an editorial everyday use, it can question token help offered in place of a sufficient response. That does not make every small contribution useless; the mismatch between the amount and the particular need is what gives the question its point.
ready_drafts.meaning_odia: କାକରର ଛୋଟ ଛୋଟ ବିନ୍ଦୁ ଓ ଭରିବାକୁ ଥିବା ଘଡ଼ା—ଏହି ଦୁଇ ମାପକୁ ପାଖାପାଖି ରଖି ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ କରାଯାଇଛି। ଅଭିଧାନ କାକର ସଂଗ୍ରହର ଅର୍ଥ ଦେବା ସହ କାକର ଚାଟିଲେ ଶୋଷ ନମେଣ୍ଟିବା ବିଷୟରେ ହିନ୍ଦୀ ପ୍ରବଚନକୁ ତୁଳନା କରିଛି। ଯେତିକି ଦରକାର, ସେଥିପାଇଁ ମିଳୁଥିବା ଅଳ୍ପଟି ଯଥେଷ୍ଟ କି ନୁହେଁ—କଥାଟି ସେଇ ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ ଉଠାଏ। ବଡ଼ ଆବଶ୍ୟକତା ଆଗରେ କେବଳ ନାମକୁ ସାହାଯ୍ୟ ଦେଲେ ଏହା କୁହାଯାଇପାରେ। ଛୋଟ ଅବଦାନକୁ ତୁଚ୍ଛ କରିବା ନୁହେଁ, ଆବଶ୍ୟକତାର ମାପ ସହ ତାହାକୁ ମିଳାଇ ଦେଖିବା ଏହି ପାଠର କଥା।
ready_drafts.english_summary: The question challenges a response too small for the need it is meant to meet.
ready_drafts.odia_summary: ଆବଶ୍ୟକତା ତୁଳନାରେ ଉପାୟଟି ଯଥେଷ୍ଟ କି ନୁହେଁ, ସେ ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ।
ready_drafts.usage_example: Original imagined example: A reading group needs enough notebooks for twenty children, but someone proposes bringing only two and calling the task finished. A volunteer quotes the dew-and-pot question, thanks them for the start, and asks how the remaining notebooks will be found. This is an invented use, not a source incident.
ready_drafts.cultural_context: The dictionary itself offers a Hindi comparison; this is not evidence of borrowing direction or a shared origin. The image is not a technical claim that dew can never be harvested. The adequacy and token-help applications are editorial readings supported by the question and comparison.
